canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Banks (as amended with effect from 1 July 2025)
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for banks in Singapore, as defined in section 2 of the Banking Act 1970. It is issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 (para 1.1), not under the Banking Act. Until 31 March 2024 the Notice was issued under the Monetary Authority of Singapore Act 1970 (section 27B); that version, dated 24 April 2015 and last revised on 1 March 2022, was cancelled with effect from 1 April 2024, when the current Notice dated 28 March 2024 took effect. MAS Notice 626 (Amendment) 2025, dated 30 June 2025, took effect on 1 July 2025 and made three changes MAS consulted on in April 2025: (a) money laundering in the Notice includes proliferation financing, so the bank's risk assessment covers proliferation financing risks (para 2.1 footnote 1; para 4.1 footnote 3); (b) the identification and verification of connected parties and beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements was revised to follow the revised FATF Recommendation 25 (paragraph 6, including paragraphs 6.14 to 6.14D); (c) a copy of an STR now goes to MAS only on request (para 14.2). Since 1 July 2025 a foreign or group entity holding only a payment services or digital token service licence is not a 'third party' a bank may rely on (para 9.1). The STR filing timelines of 5 business days, or 1 business day for sanctioned parties, are in the Guidelines to the Notice, not in the Notice.

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 1.1: "This Notice is issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 824 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Finance Companies
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for finance companies licensed under section 6 of the Finance Companies Act 1967 (para 1.1). It is not the Notice for approved trustees, which is MAS Notice SFA13-N01. Issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022; dated 30 June 2025 and in effect from 1 July 2025 (para 1.2). As in the other AML/CFT Notices amended in 2025, money laundering in it includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 824 para 1.1: "applies to all finance companies in Singapore, as licensed under section 6 of the Finance Companies Act 1967"

canonical_name: MAS Notice SFA04-N02 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Capital Markets Intermediaries
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for holders of a capital markets services licence under the Securities and Futures Act 2001 and for persons exempted under paragraphs 3(1)(d), 3A(1)(d) and 7(1)(b) of the Second Schedule to the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations (para 1.1). Issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022; dated 30 June 2025 and in effect from 1 July 2025 (para 1.2). Financial advisers have their own Notice, FAA-N06. Money laundering in it includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice SFA04-N02 para 1.1: "holders of a capital markets services licence under the Securities and Futures Act 2001"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 314 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Direct Life Insurers
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for direct life insurers licensed under section 11 of the Insurance Act 1966 (para 1.1). Apart from paragraphs 13.3 to 13.9, it applies only to the insurer's business concerned with life policies and excludes the reinsurance of liabilities under life policies (para 1.2). Issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022; dated 30 June 2025 and in effect from 1 July 2025 (para 1.3). Money laundering in it includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 314 para 1.1: "applies to all direct life insurers licensed under section 11 of the Insurance Act 1966"

canonical_name: MAS Notices PSN01 and PSN02 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Holders of a Payment Services Licence
description: Two AML/CFT Notices, each issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, dated 2 April 2024, in effect from 4 April 2024 and last revised on 30 June 2025 (amendment in effect from 1 July 2025). PSN01 applies to licensees under the Payment Services Act 2019 that carry on a business of providing a specified payment service — an account issuance, domestic money transfer, cross-border money transfer or money-changing service — and to persons exempt under section 13(1) of that Act that offer a specified product. PSN02 applies to every payment services licensee that carries on a business of providing a digital payment token service. Both require suspicious transaction reports to STRO, and in both money laundering includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice PSN02 para 1.1: "that carry on a business of providing a digital payment token service"

canonical_name: MAS Notice VCC-N01 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Variable Capital Companies
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for variable capital companies. Unlike the other AML/CFT Notices it is issued under section 84 of the Variable Capital Companies Act 2018, not under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, and it applies to all VCCs under that Act (para 1.1). Dated and in effect from 14 January 2020; last revised on 30 June 2025, with MAS Notice VCC-N01 (Amendment) 2025 in effect from 1 July 2025. Money laundering in it includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice VCC-N01 para 1.1: "This Notice is issued pursuant to section 84 of the Variable Capital Companies 2018"

canonical_name: MAS Notice FSM-N27 — Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Holders of Digital Token Service Licence
description: MAS's AML/CFT Notice for digital token service providers: it applies to holders of a licence granted under section 138 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 and is issued under section 16 of that Act (para 1.1). Dated 30 May 2025, in effect from 30 June 2025 (para 1.2), last revised on 30 June 2025 with the amendment in effect from 1 July 2025. It covers the risk assessment, new products and technologies, customer due diligence, simplified and enhanced measures, reliance on third parties, correspondent accounts, agency arrangements, value transfers, record keeping, suspicious transaction reporting to STRO, and internal policies, compliance, audit and training; money laundering in it includes proliferation financing (footnote 1).

metadata.issued_under: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, section 16
metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice FSM-N27 para 1.1: "applies to a holder of a licen ce granted under section 138 of the FSM Act"

canonical_name: Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 (FSMA)
description: A cross-sector Act giving MAS powers over financial institutions generally. Its Parts cover: general powers over financial institutions (Part 2); prohibition orders (Part 3); directions or regulations to discharge obligations binding on Singapore by a UN Security Council decision (section 15) and requirements for the prevention of money laundering and terrorism financing (section 16, under which most MAS AML/CFT Notices are issued) (Part 4); an information-sharing scheme for prescribed financial institutions (Part 4A); technology risk management (Part 5, section 29); dispute resolution schemes (Part 6); control and resolution of financial institutions (Parts 7 and 8); digital token service providers (Part 9); inspection and investigation (Parts 10 and 10A). It commenced in phases: Phase 1 on 28 April 2023, Phase 2A on 10 May 2024, Phase 2B on 31 July 2024 and Phase 3 (Part 9) on 30 June 2025.

metadata.source_quote: FSMA section 16(1): "The Authority may, from time to time, issue such directions, or make such regulations under section 192, concerning any financial institution or class of financial institutions as the Authority considers necessary for the prevention of money laundering or the financing of terrorism."

canonical_name: FSMA Part 9 — Digital Token Service Providers (sections 136 to 167)
description: Licensing and supervision of Singapore-based providers of digital token services outside Singapore. An individual or partnership must not, from a place of business in Singapore, carry on a business of providing any type of digital token service outside Singapore without a licence (s.137(1)); a Singapore corporation, including a limited liability partnership, must not carry on such a business, whether from Singapore or elsewhere, without a licence (s.137(3), s.137(7)). Businesses licensed or exempted under the Securities and Futures Act 2001, the Financial Advisers Act 2001 or the Payment Services Act 2019 for the relevant activity are excluded (s.137(5)). Part 9 came into force on 30 June 2025 with no transitional arrangement: providers caught by s.137 had to suspend or cease their services outside Singapore by that date, and MAS said it would grant a licence only in extremely limited circumstances (MAS response to feedback, 30 May 2025). AML/CFT duties are in MAS Notice FSM-N27; technology risk in MAS Notice FSM-N30.

metadata.source_quote: FSMA section 137(3): "a Singapore corporation must not carry on a business, whether from Singapore or elsewhere, of providing any type of digital token service outside Singapore unless the Singapore corporation has in force a licence."

canonical_name: Payment Services Act 2019 (PSA)
description: Singapore's payment services statute, in force from 28 January 2020 (except sections 111, 113 and 114). It regulates seven payment services (First Schedule Part 1): account issuance, domestic money transfer, cross-border money transfer, merchant acquisition, e-money issuance, digital payment token and money-changing services. There are three licence classes: money-changing, standard payment institution and major payment institution (s.6(2)); a major payment institution licence is needed above the transaction-value thresholds in s.6(5), e.g. a monthly average over a calendar year exceeding S$3 million for any one of the listed services or S$6 million for two or more. Amendments by Act 1 of 2021 in force from 4 April 2024 widened the digital payment token service to include custody and transmission services (s.2(1)) and added s.21A, under which regulations set customer-asset safeguarding and other requirements for DPT service providers.

metadata.source_quote: PSA section 6(2): "( a ) a money‑changing licence; ( b ) a standard payment institution licence; ( c ) a major payment institution licence."

canonical_name: Securities and Futures Act 2001
description: Singapore's capital markets statute (formerly cited as Cap. 289). Its Parts include organised markets, clearing facilities, the central depository system, holders of a capital markets services licence and their representatives (Part 4), conduct of business, disclosure of interests, short selling, market conduct (Part 12) and offers of investments (Part 13). Collective investment schemes authorised under section 286 have approved trustees under section 289. MAS's AML/CFT Notices for capital markets intermediaries (SFA04-N02) and approved trustees (SFA13-N01) take their scope from this Act but are issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022.

canonical_name: Banking Act 1970
description: Singapore's banking statute (formerly cited as Cap. 19). It provides for the licensing of banks (Part 3) and of merchant banks (Part 7B), and for credit card and charge card businesses (Part 8). MAS Notice 637 on risk-based capital adequacy requirements for banks incorporated in Singapore is issued under sections 10(2), 10A(1), 10B(1) and 65(2) of this Act. MAS Notice 626 applies to banks as defined in section 2 of this Act but is issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, not under the Banking Act.

canonical_name: Insurance Act 1966
description: Singapore's insurance statute (formerly cited as Cap. 142). Its Parts cover the conduct of insurance business, foreign insurer schemes, insurance intermediaries, returns, inspections, investigations, winding up and transfers of business. Direct life insurers licensed under section 11 are subject to MAS Notice 314, which is issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, not under this Act.

canonical_name: Financial Advisers Act 2001
description: Singapore's financial advisory statute (formerly cited as Cap. 110). Its Parts cover financial advisers and representatives, conduct of business, accounts and audit, prohibited businesses, MAS's powers, supervision and investigation, and offences. Licensed financial advisers and certain exempt financial advisers are subject to MAS Notice FAA-N06 on AML/CFT, issued under section 16 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022.

canonical_name: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA)
description: Singapore's data protection statute. Its data protection provisions came into force on 2 July 2014 and the Do Not Call provisions on 2 January 2014. The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2020 added mandatory data breach notification (Part 6A) for breaches on or after 1 February 2021, and raised the maximum financial penalty under section 48J to 10% of annual turnover in Singapore for an organisation whose turnover there exceeds S$10 million (otherwise S$1 million), for contraventions from 1 October 2022. Nothing in Parts 3 to 6B affects obligations imposed by or under the law, and other written law prevails where it is inconsistent with those Parts (s.4(6)). The Info-communications Media Development Authority is designated as the Personal Data Protection Commission (s.5). PDPC guidance includes the Advisory Guidelines on the PDPA for Children's Personal Data in the Digital Environment (28 March 2024).

metadata.source_quote: PDPA section 48J(3)(a): "by an organisation whose annual turnover in Singapore exceeds $10 million — 10% of the annual turnover in Singapore of the organisation"

canonical_name: MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines (January 2021) — Guidelines on Risk Management Practices – Technology Risk
description: MAS guidelines issued on 18 January 2021 setting risk management principles and practices for technology risk. Chapters cover technology risk governance and oversight (including appointing a Chief Information Officer, Chief Technology Officer or head of IT, and a Chief Information Security Officer or head of information security), the technology risk management framework, IT project management and security-by-design, software application development, IT service management (incident and problem management), IT resilience, access control, cryptography, data and infrastructure security, cyber security operations, cyber security assessment, online financial services and IT audit. They are guidelines; the binding incident-notification and availability rules are in MAS Notices on technology risk management, such as FSM-N05 for banks and FSM-N30 for digital token service providers.

canonical_name: MAS Guidelines on Business Continuity Management (June 2022)
description: MAS guidelines issued on 6 June 2022, replacing the 2003 BCM Guidelines and a 2006 circular. They contain sound BCM principles that financial institutions are encouraged to adopt, commensurate with their nature, size, risk profile and complexity. Chapters cover critical business services and functions, Service Recovery Time Objectives, dependency mapping, concentration risk, continuous review and improvement, testing, audit, incident and crisis management, and the responsibilities of the board and senior management. MAS expected a BCM audit plan within 12 months of issuance and the first BCM audit within 24 months.

canonical_name: MAS Guidelines on Outsourcing (Banks) and Guidelines on Outsourcing (Financial Institutions other than Banks)
description: Two sets of MAS outsourcing guidelines. The Guidelines on Outsourcing (Banks), published 11 December 2023 and effective 11 December 2024, apply to banks and merchant banks alongside the binding MAS Notices 658 and 1121 on management of outsourced relevant services. The Guidelines on Outsourcing (Financial Institutions other than Banks), in their January 2025 version, apply to other MAS-regulated institutions and ask for a register of outsourcing arrangements to be submitted to MAS at least annually or on request. Both cover board and senior management responsibilities, evaluation of risks, assessment of service providers, outsourcing agreements, confidentiality and security, business continuity, monitoring and control, audit and inspection, and outsourcing outside Singapore and within a group, with an annex on cloud computing; the banks' Guidelines also cover the use of sub-contractors.

canonical_name: Variable Capital Companies Act 2018
description: Provides for the incorporation, operation and regulation of variable capital companies, a corporate structure for collective investment schemes; in force from 14 January 2020. An umbrella VCC may have sub-funds whose assets and liabilities are segregated (s.29). A VCC's manager must be a holder of a capital markets services licence for fund management, a person mentioned in section 99(1)(a) to (d) of the Securities and Futures Act 2001, or a prescribed person. The Act is administered by ACRA; under section 84 MAS may issue AML/CFT directions to VCCs, which it has done in MAS Notice VCC-N01.

metadata.source_quote: VCC Act section 84(1): "MAS may, from time to time, issue such directions or make such regulations concerning any VCC or class of VCCs as MAS considers necessary for the prevention of money laundering, the financing of terrorism or proliferation financing."

canonical_name: Workplace Fairness Act 2025
description: Protects individuals against discrimination by employers on the ground of protected characteristics and establishes fair employment practices. The protected characteristics are age, nationality, sex, marital status, pregnancy, caregiving responsibilities, race, religion, language ability, disability and mental health condition (s.8). It does not apply to employers with fewer than the prescribed number of employees, set at 25 (s.4, except section 26). It is not yet in force: it comes into operation on a date the Minister appoints, and MOM has said it aims for the Act to take effect in end-2027. Under the companion Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Act 2025, parties must attempt mediation before a claim proceeds to the Employment Claims Tribunals (claims up to S$250,000) or the High Court.

metadata.source_quote: Workplace Fairness Act 2025 section 8: "( a ) age; ( b ) nationality; ( c ) sex; ( d ) marital status; ( e ) pregnancy; ( f ) caregiving responsibilities; ( g ) race; ( h ) religion; ( i ) language ability; ( j ) disability; and ( k ) mental health condition."

canonical_name: SGX sustainability reporting rules and the ACRA / SGX RegCo climate reporting timeline
description: SGX Mainboard Rule 711A requires every listed issuer to prepare an annual sustainability report describing its practices with reference to the primary components in Rule 711B on a 'comply or explain' basis; climate-related disclosures are a primary component that may not be excluded. Under the timeline ACRA and SGX RegCo announced on 25 August 2025: Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions reporting is mandatory for all listed companies from FY2025; other ISSB-based climate-related disclosures are mandatory for Straits Times Index constituents from FY2025, for other listed companies with market capitalisation of S$1 billion or more from FY2028 and for the rest from FY2030; Scope 3 reporting is mandatory for STI constituents from FY2026 and voluntary for others; external limited assurance on Scope 1 and 2 is deferred to FY2029. For large non-listed companies, ISSB-based climate disclosures are deferred to FY2030 and assurance to FY2032.

canonical_name: Prevention of Corruption Act 1960
description: Singapore's anti-corruption statute, covering corrupt solicitation, receipt, giving or offering of gratification in the public and private sectors (s.5) and corrupt transactions with agents (s.6). The base penalty is a fine of up to S$100,000, imprisonment of up to 5 years, or both; it rises to 7 years where the matter concerns a contract with the Government or a public body (s.7), and for some offences involving Members of Parliament and public bodies. The Act applies to Singapore citizens outside as well as within Singapore (s.37). CPIB investigates; prosecutions need the consent of the Public Prosecutor (s.33).

metadata.source_quote: PCA section 37(1): "The provisions of this Act have effect, in relation to citizens of Singapore, outside as well as within Singapore"

canonical_name: Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (CDSA)
description: Singapore's principal money laundering statute, in force from 30 November 1993. Section numbers below are those of the 2020 Revised Edition. Section 5 establishes the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office. Section 45 requires a person who knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect, in the course of trade, profession, business or employment, that property represents proceeds of, or was or is intended to be used in connection with, drug dealing or criminal conduct to disclose it to a Suspicious Transaction Reporting Officer as soon as reasonably practicable, whether or not the transaction was completed (fine up to S$250,000 and/or 3 years for an individual; up to S$500,000 otherwise). The money laundering offences are in sections 50 to 55A and tipping-off in section 57.

metadata.source_quote: CDSA section 45(1): "the person must disclose the knowledge or suspicion or the information or other matter on which that knowledge or suspicion is based to a Suspicious Transaction Reporting Officer as soon as is reasonably practicable after it comes to the person’s attention."

canonical_name: MAS targeted financial sanctions regulations (FSMA section 15) and the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act 2002
description: The duties to freeze, and not to deal with, the funds and assets of designated persons do not come from the AML/CFT Notices. For financial institutions they come from MAS's regulations under section 192 read with section 15(1)(b) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022, which give effect to UN Security Council decisions (the 'FSM Sanctions Regulations'; for proliferation financing, the Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 identify those on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and Iran as currently relevant), and from the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act 2002, which prohibits dealing with property of terrorists (s.6), imposes a duty to disclose (s.8) and makes tipping-off an offence (s.10B). The Notices require screening against MAS's lists and enhanced measures that take these regulations into account.

metadata.legal_basis: FSMA s.15(1)(b) and s.192; TSOFA ss.6, 8, 10B
metadata.source_quote: FSMA section 15(1): "as the Authority considers necessary in order to discharge or facilitate the discharge of any obligation binding on Singapore by virtue of a decision of the Security Council of the United Nations."

canonical_name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)
description: Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator, covering banking, capital markets, insurance and payments. It administers the Monetary Authority of Singapore Act 1970 and the sector statutes (Banking Act 1970, Insurance Act 1966, Securities and Futures Act 2001, Financial Advisers Act 2001, Payment Services Act 2019, Financial Services and Markets Act 2022), issues the AML/CFT Notices and supervises financial institutions' compliance with them, including VCCs' under the Variable Capital Companies Act 2018.

metadata.type: Central bank and integrated financial regulator

canonical_name: Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO)
description: Singapore's Financial Intelligence Unit, established by section 5 of the CDSA and located in the Commercial Affairs Department of the Singapore Police Force. It receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports, cash movement reports and cash transaction reports. STRO was admitted to the Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units in June 2002.

metadata.parent: Singapore Police Force — Commercial Affairs Department

canonical_name: Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC)
description: The Info-communications Media Development Authority (IMDA) is designated as the Personal Data Protection Commission under section 5 of the PDPA. The PDPC administers and enforces the PDPA, including financial penalties under section 48J, issues advisory guidelines (for example on children's personal data, 28 March 2024) and released the Model AI Governance Framework (second edition, 21 January 2020).

canonical_name: Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA)
description: The national regulator of business entities, public accountants and corporate service providers in Singapore, formed on 1 April 2004. It administers, among others, the Companies Act 1967, the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2005, the Accountants Act 2004, the Variable Capital Companies Act 2018 and the Corporate Service Providers Act 2024 (under which corporate service providers must register with ACRA from 9 June 2025), and keeps the Central Register of Registrable Controllers.

canonical_name: Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB)
description: Singapore's anti-corruption agency, established in 1952, under the Prime Minister's Office with its Director reporting to the Prime Minister. It is the only agency authorised to investigate corruption offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act 1960, in the public and private sectors; prosecutions under that Act need the consent of the Public Prosecutor.

canonical_name: Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS)
description: Singapore's competition and consumer protection authority. Its cases cover anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance and mergers under the Competition Act 2004, and unfair practices under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003.

canonical_name: Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)
description: Singapore's tax authority. For international tax cooperation, Singapore-based financial institutions report financial account information to IRAS under the Common Reporting Standard (Singapore committed to begin automatic exchange in 2018; financial institutions establish customers' tax residence with effect from 1 January 2017) and, since 2015, information on accounts of specified US persons under FATCA, which IRAS passes to the US Internal Revenue Service. IRAS is not an AML/CFT supervisor of financial institutions.

canonical_name: Ministry of Manpower (MOM)
description: The ministry responsible for the Workplace Fairness Act 2025, which provides for a Commissioner for Workplace Fairness (s.37) and which MOM aims to bring into force in end-2027. Workplace discrimination claims are heard after mediation by the Employment Claims Tribunals (up to S$250,000) or the High Court, not by a separate workplace fairness tribunal.

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — proliferation financing within the risk assessment (from 1 July 2025)
description: Since MAS Notice 626 (Amendment) 2025 took effect on 1 July 2025, money laundering in the Notice includes proliferation financing and every reference to money laundering risks is read accordingly (para 2.1 footnote 1); the risks a bank must identify, assess and understand under para 4.1 include proliferation financing risks (footnote 3). PF therefore runs through the risk assessment, CDD, screening and suspicious transaction reporting rather than being a separate regime. MAS has said PF risk assessments may be done on their own or as part of the existing ML/TF risk assessments, and should be done as soon as possible if not already in place. The change follows the FATF's October 2020 amendments to Recommendations 1 and 2, which require countries and the private sector to identify and assess the risk of potential breach, non-implementation or evasion of the proliferation-related targeted financial sanctions in Recommendation 7, and to mitigate it.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 2.1 footnote 1: "In this Notice, money laundering includes proliferation financing, and all references in this Notice to money laundering (including money laundering risks) shall be construed accordingly."

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — risk assessment and risk mitigation (paragraphs 4 and 5)
description: A bank must take appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand its money laundering and terrorism financing risks in relation to its customers, the countries its customers are from or in, the countries it operates in, and its products, services, transactions (including digital token transactions) and delivery channels (para 4.1). Those steps include documenting the risk assessments, considering all relevant risk factors before deciding the overall risk level and mitigation, keeping the assessments up to date and having mechanisms to provide them to MAS (para 4.2). Policies, procedures and controls to manage the risks must be approved by senior management, monitored and enhanced where necessary, with enhanced measures where higher risks are identified (para 4.3). New products, business practices, delivery mechanisms and technologies must be risk-assessed before launch or use (para 5). The Notice sets no fixed review frequency.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 4.2(c): "keeping the bank’s risk assessments up-to-date"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — customer due diligence (paragraph 6)
description: CDD is performed when a bank establishes business relations; undertakes, for a customer without business relations, a transaction exceeding S$20,000 (other than a digital token transaction), any digital token transaction, any domestic wire transfer, a cross-border wire transfer exceeding S$1,500 or any digital token value transfer; suspects money laundering or terrorism financing; or doubts information previously obtained (para 6.3). The bank identifies and verifies the customer using reliable, independent source data, documents or information (paras 6.5-6.9), identifies connected parties of a legal person or arrangement (para 6.8) and persons acting for the customer (paras 6.10-6.11), inquires whether there is any beneficial owner (para 6.13), identifies beneficial owners (para 6.14) and takes reasonable steps to verify them (para 6.14B); the Notice sets no ownership percentage. It understands the purpose and intended nature of the relationship (para 6.18) and monitors business relations on an ongoing basis (para 6.19). Reliance on third parties is allowed only under paragraph 9, never for ongoing monitoring.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 6.13: "Subject to paragraph 6.16, a bank shall inquire if there exists any beneficial owner in relation to a customer."

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — enhanced CDD for higher-risk customers (paragraphs 8.5-8.8 and 10)
description: A bank must have systems to determine whether a customer presents a higher ML/TF risk (para 8.5). Higher-risk circumstances include a customer or beneficial owner from or in a jurisdiction for which the FATF has called for countermeasures (to be treated as higher risk), or one known to have inadequate AML/CFT measures (para 8.6). The enhanced measures of para 8.3 — senior management approval, source of wealth and source of funds, enhanced ongoing monitoring — apply to customers the bank determines, or MAS or other Singapore authorities notify, as higher risk (para 8.7), and must take account of the laws, regulations and directions MAS administers, including sanctions regulations (para 8.8). Correspondent banking requires additional measures (para 10).

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 8.7: "A bank shall perform the appropriate enhanced CDD measures in paragraph 8.3 for business relations with or transactions for any customer"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — politically exposed persons (paragraphs 8.1-8.4)
description: A bank must determine whether a customer, a person acting for it, a connected party or a beneficial owner is a politically exposed person or a family member or close associate of one (para 8.2). For them it must at least obtain senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship, establish source of wealth and source of funds by appropriate and reasonable means, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring (para 8.3). A risk-based approach to whether, and how far, to apply those measures is allowed only for domestic PEPs, international organisation PEPs and PEPs who have stepped down (considering their continuing influence), with their family members and close associates, and not where the relationship presents a higher risk (para 8.4). Foreign PEPs therefore always receive enhanced CDD. The Notice has no separate category of 'Singapore Government PEPs' and sets no fixed period after a PEP leaves office.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 8.3(a): "obtain approval from the bank’s senior management to establish or continue business relations with, or undertake any transaction without an account being opened for the customer"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — source of wealth and source of funds (paragraph 8.3(b))
description: For PEPs and other higher-risk customers a bank must establish, by appropriate and reasonable means, the source of wealth and source of funds of the customer and any beneficial owner (para 8.3(b), applied by para 8.7). The Guidelines to the Notice explain that source of wealth refers to the origin of the customer's and beneficial owner's entire body of wealth and how it was acquired, distinct from identifying the assets they own (Guidelines 8-5-5), and source of funds to the origin of the particular funds or assets that are the subject of the business relations (Guidelines 8-5-6).

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 8.3(b): "establish, by appropriate and reasonable means, the source of wealth and source of funds of the customer and any beneficial owner of the customer"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — suspicious transaction reporting (paragraph 14)
description: A bank must keep in mind the CDSA and TSOFA provisions on reporting suspicious transactions and have internal policies to meet them, including a single reference point for internal referrals and records of all transactions referred to STRO with the internal findings (para 14.1). It must promptly submit suspicious transaction reports, including on attempted transactions and regardless of amount, to STRO and give MAS a copy on request (para 14.2, as amended from 1 July 2025: previously a copy of every STR went to MAS). It must consider, and document, whether to file where it cannot complete CDD or the customer is reluctant, withdraws or ends the relationship (para 14.3), and where CDD would tip off the customer it may stop, must document why and must file an STR (para 14.4). Tipping-off is an offence under CDSA s.57 and TSOFA s.10B. The Guidelines to the Notice (as revised with effect from 1 July 2025) expect an STR to be filed no later than 5 business days after suspicion was first established, and no later than 1 business day for sanctioned parties and those acting for them. The 2025 amendments did not change what triggers an STR or prescribe STR content.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 14.2: "A bank shall promptly submit reports on suspicious transactions (including attempted transactions), regardless of the amount of the transaction, to STRO, and extend a copy to the Authority upon request."

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — screening (paragraphs 6.39-6.42) and sanctions
description: A bank must screen customers, persons acting for them, connected parties and beneficial owners against relevant ML/TF information sources and the lists and information provided by MAS or other Singapore authorities (para 6.39): at onboarding, for occasional transactions, periodically and when the lists or the persons change (para 6.40); screen originators and beneficiaries of wire and value transfers (para 6.41); and document the results (para 6.42). Enhanced CDD must take account of MAS's sanctions regulations and directions (para 8.8). The duty to freeze designated persons' assets without delay comes from MAS's sanctions regulations under FSMA section 15 and from the TSOFA, not from the Notice; the Guidelines expect an STR on a positive sanctions hit no later than 1 business day after suspicion is established.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 6.39: "against relevant money laundering and terrorism financing information sources, as well as li sts and information provided by the Authority or other relevant authorities in Singapore"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — internal policies, compliance and audit (paragraph 15)
description: A bank must develop and implement adequate internal policies, procedures and controls, taking account of its ML/TF risks and the size of its business, and communicate them to employees (para 15.1); they must meet all the Notice's requirements (para 15.2). A Singapore-incorporated bank must apply a group AML/CFT policy to its branches and subsidiaries (paras 15.3-15.9). It must appoint an AML/CFT compliance officer at the management level (para 15.10) who is suitably qualified, adequately resourced and has timely access to customer records (para 15.11); maintain an adequately resourced, independent audit function that regularly assesses the policies and compliance (para 15.12); and screen employees and officers when hiring (para 15.13). The Notice sets no annual review cycle and requires no alternate compliance officer.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 15.10: "the appointment of an AML/CFT compliance officer at the management level"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — training (paragraph 15.14)
description: A bank must take all appropriate steps to ensure its employees and officers, in Singapore or elsewhere, are regularly and appropriately trained on AML/CFT laws and regulations, in particular CDD measures and detecting and reporting suspicious transactions; prevailing money laundering and terrorism financing techniques, methods and trends (money laundering including proliferation financing); and the bank's internal AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls and their own roles and responsibilities (para 15.14). Training records and effectiveness testing are good practice that the Notice does not itself prescribe.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 15.14: "are regularly and appropriately trained on"

canonical_name: MAS Notice 626 — record keeping, at least 5 years (paragraph 12)
description: A bank must prepare, maintain and retain records of all data, documents and information the Notice requires (para 12.1) so that legal requirements are met, any individual transaction can be reconstructed as evidence, authorities and auditors can review compliance and enquiries can be answered in a reasonable time (para 12.2). CDD information, account files, business correspondence and results of analysis are kept for at least 5 years after the business relations end or the wire transfer, value transfer or transaction is completed, and transaction records for at least 5 years after the transaction (para 12.3). Records about a matter under investigation or the subject of an STR are kept as STRO or other authorities request (para 12.5).

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice 626 para 12.3(a): "a period of at least 5 years following the termination of such business relations or completion of such wire transfers, value transfers or transactions"

canonical_name: DTSP scope — digital token services provided outside Singapore (FSMA s.136-137, First Schedule)
description: Part 9 catches an individual or partnership operating from a place of business in Singapore, and any Singapore corporation (including an LLP) wherever it operates, that carries on a business of providing digital token services outside Singapore (s.137(1), (3)). A digital token service provided alongside another business is presumed to be a business of its own, and proof that it is related or incidental does not rebut that (s.137(2), (4)). 'Digital token' covers digital payment tokens and digital representations of capital markets products (s.136(1)). The First Schedule lists ten services: dealing; facilitating exchange; accepting tokens for transmission; arranging transmission; inducing persons to buy or sell; safeguarding tokens or digital token instruments the provider controls; carrying out customer instructions over them; and advice or research on the sale of digital tokens. Technical service providers that never possess money or tokens, central bank digital token services and limited purpose tokens are excluded. A person required to be licensed, approved or recognised, or exempted, under the SFA, the FAA or the Payment Services Act 2019 for the relevant activity is outside s.137, as are persons in the Second Schedule and prescribed classes (s.137(5)).

metadata.source_quote: FSMA section 137(1): "an individual or a partnership must not from a place of business in Singapore carry on a business of providing any type of digital token service outside Singapore unless the individual or the partnership has in force a licence."

canonical_name: DTSP licensing (FSMA s.138-147)
description: MAS may grant a licence with or without conditions or refuse one, after giving the applicant a chance to be heard (s.138(2), (5)). It must not grant one unless the applicant has a permanent place of business in Singapore, a Singapore-resident executive director (corporation) or partner or manager (partnership or LLP) unless a prescribed exception applies, meets the prescribed financial requirements and the operational requirements MAS specifies, and MAS is satisfied it is fit and proper, as to its financial condition, that the public interest will be served and as to any other relevant criteria (s.138(3)). A licensee must keep meeting financial and operational requirements (s.138(6)), keep a permanent place of business and books (s.143), notify MAS of specified events (s.144), report to MAS (ss.145-146) and must not grant credit facilities to individuals in Singapore (s.147). Unlicensed business is an offence: up to S$125,000 and/or 3 years for an individual, up to S$250,000 otherwise, with daily fines for continuing offences (s.137(6)). MAS said it would grant a licence only in extremely limited circumstances.

metadata.source_quote: FSMA section 147(1): "A licensee must not carry on a business of granting any credit facility to any individual in Singapore."

canonical_name: PSA digital payment token user protection — safeguarding (from 4 October 2024) and consumer access measures (from 19 June 2025)
description: From 4 April 2024 the amended Payment Services Act 2019 brought DPT custody and transmission services within the DPT service (s.2(1)) and empowered MAS to impose safeguarding and other requirements on DPT service providers by regulation (s.21A). The Payment Services Regulations on safeguarding customers' assets took effect six months later: customers' assets must be segregated and held in a trust account for their benefit, with proper books and records and effective controls (PS Regulations reg 18B). MAS Guidelines PS-G03 (issued 2 April 2024, last revised 19 September 2024) set out the expectations: Chapters 1 to 3 (safeguarding) from 4 October 2024; from 19 June 2025 Chapters 4 to 6 — a risk awareness assessment before a retail customer may access DPT services, no incentives to entice retail customers or to have others promote or refer services to them, no credit facility, loan of DPTs, leveraged DPT transactions or DPT derivatives contracts for retail customers, management of conflicts of interest, DPT listing and governance policies, and complaints handling.

metadata.source_quote: Guidelines PS-G03 para 1.2.1: "Chapters 1, 2 (other than paragraphs 2.3.1 to 2.3.7), 3 and paragraph 5.3 of the Guidelines take effect on 4 October 2024."

canonical_name: PDPA mandatory data breach notification (Part 6A, from 1 February 2021)
description: For a data breach on or after 1 February 2021, an organisation that has reason to believe a breach has occurred must assess, reasonably and expeditiously, whether it is notifiable (s.26C). A breach is notifiable if it results, or is likely to result, in significant harm to an affected individual, or is or is likely to be of a significant scale (s.26B) — 500 or more affected individuals under the PDP (Notification of Data Breaches) Regulations 2021, as the PDPC's guide states. A breach only within the organisation is not notifiable (s.26B(4)). The PDPC must be notified as soon as practicable and no later than 3 calendar days after the organisation assesses the breach as notifiable (s.26D(1)); affected individuals must be notified, on or after notifying the PDPC, where significant harm is likely, unless remedial action or prior measures make harm unlikely or an authority directs otherwise (s.26D(2), (5)-(7)). Contraventions can attract the section 48J financial penalties.

metadata.source_quote: PDPA section 26D(1): "the organisation must notify the Commission as soon as is practicable, but in any case no later than 3 calendar days after the day the organisation makes that assessment."

canonical_name: PDPC Model AI Governance Framework (second edition, 21 January 2020)
description: A voluntary framework released by the PDPC (first edition 2019; second edition 21 January 2020) for private-sector organisations deploying AI at scale. It gives guidance in four areas: internal governance structures and measures; determining the level of human involvement in AI-augmented decision-making (human-in-the-loop, human-out-of-the-loop and human-over-the-loop approaches); operations management; and stakeholder interaction and communication. It does not amend the PDPA.

metadata.source_quote: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd ed.) para 2.3: "This voluntary Model Framework provides guidance on the key issues to be considered and measures that can be implemented."

canonical_name: MAS technology risk and cyber resilience — TRM Guidelines plus the binding TRM Notices
description: The TRM Guidelines (January 2021) set expectations: the board and senior management should appoint a Chief Information Officer (or CTO or head of IT) and a Chief Information Security Officer (or head of information security), establish a technology risk management framework, apply security-by-design, maintain incident and problem management, IT resilience and disaster recovery testing, access controls (multi-factor authentication for sensitive system functions and remote access), cryptography, data and infrastructure security, cyber security operations and assessments (vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, cyber exercises). The binding rules sit in MAS Notices: for banks, MAS Notice FSM-N05 (in effect 10 May 2024, issued under FSMA s.29) requires critical systems to be identified, unscheduled downtime of each critical system not to exceed 4 hours in any 12 months, a recovery time objective of not more than 4 hours validated at least once every 12 months, notification to MAS within 1 hour of discovering a relevant incident, and a root cause and impact analysis report within 14 days. MAS Notice FSM-N30 sets the same pattern for digital token service providers.

metadata.source_quote: MAS Notice FSM-N05 para 7: "A Bank must notify the Authority as soon as possible, but not later than 1 hour, upon the discovery of a relevant incident."

canonical_name: MAS BCM Guidelines — business continuity expectations
description: Financial institutions should identify critical business services and functions; set a Service Recovery Time Objective for each critical business service; map end-to-end dependencies on people, processes, technology and third parties; manage concentration risk; test plans regularly against severe but plausible disruption scenarios; audit the BCM framework and each critical business service's BCM at least once every three years by a qualified, independent party; and have incident and crisis management arrangements. Senior management should give the board an annual attestation on the state of BCM preparedness, its alignment with the Guidelines and key issues such as significant residual risk, and provide it to MAS on request (para 10.6). The Guidelines are principles FIs are encouraged to adopt proportionately, not a binding Notice.

metadata.source_quote: MAS BCM Guidelines para 10.6: "The senior management should provide an annual attestation to the Board on the state of the FI’s BCM preparedness"

canonical_name: Register of Registrable Controllers (RORC) and ACRA's Central RORC
description: Companies (private and public), foreign companies registered in Singapore and LLPs must keep a private register of their registrable controllers and, since 30 July 2020, file that information with ACRA's Central Register of Registrable Controllers; from 16 June 2025 a newly incorporated or registered entity files on the day of registration. For a company with share capital, a person has a significant interest with an interest in more than 25% of the shares or shares carrying more than 25% of the total voting power, and significant control with the right to appoint or remove directors holding a majority of voting rights, more than 25% of the voting rights, or the right or ability to exercise significant influence or control. The Central RORC is not public: access is limited to the entity's officers and corporate service providers and to law enforcement agencies administering or enforcing laws under their purview.

canonical_name: STR filing through SONAR
description: Suspicious transaction reports must be filed electronically through the STRO Online Notices And Reporting platform (SONAR), which is also used for cross-border cash movement reports and precious stones and metals dealers' cash transaction reports. Under CDSA section 5 STRO receives and analyses these reports. An STR filed with STRO also meets the reporting obligation under the TSOFA (Guidelines to MAS Notice 626, para 14-2).

canonical_name: MAS AML enforcement actions — 1MDB (2016-2017) and the August 2023 money laundering case
description: On 30 May 2017 MAS completed its two-year review of banks involved in 1MDB-related transactions: financial penalties of S$29.1 million in aggregate had been imposed on eight banks (BSI Bank, Falcon Bank, DBS, UBS AG, Standard Chartered Bank, Coutts, Credit Suisse and UOB), and MAS shut down two merchant banks, BSI Bank and Falcon Bank. The penalties on Credit Suisse (S$0.7 million) and UOB (S$0.9 million) were for breaches of MAS Notice 626. After the money laundering case of August 2023 — ten persons arrested in police raids on 15 August 2023, all ten convicted and sentenced by June 2024 — MAS on 4 July 2025 imposed composition penalties totalling S$27.45 million on nine financial institutions (banks, capital markets services licensees and a trust company) for AML/CFT breaches related to the case, and issued prohibition orders against four individuals.
